analysis.one_liner: Blocks states from requiring overtime pay for farm workers working under 60 hours a week.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have overridden state overtime rules for farm workers, died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law generally does not require overtime pay for agricultural workers, but a few states have stepped in with their own rules. This bill would amend federal law to block any state from setting a maximum farm workweek below 60 hours, wiping out stricter state overtime protections. It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Farm employers and agribusiness operators in states that require overtime for agricultural workers below 60 hours a week, who would no longer owe overtime pay and could schedule long weeks at straight time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farm employers in states with overtime rules

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so that federal law preempts any state law setting a maximum agricultural workweek of less than 60 hours [S2][S3].
Because federal law generally exempts agricultural employees from overtime requirements entirely, the bill would make the 60-hour mark the floor everywhere, replacing stricter state standards [S2].
Supporters could argue a single national threshold replaces a patchwork of state rules that falls hardest on smaller farms operating across state lines [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Farm workers in states that have set maximum workweeks below 60 hours would lose the overtime pay those state laws provide, and would face longer weeks at straight time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm workers in states with overtime rules

drawbacks.text: Farm workers in states with overtime protections would lose overtime wages they currently earn, since federal law provides them no overtime rights at all [S2].
The bill overrides state labor laws that states chose to enact for one of the lowest-paid and most physically demanding workforces, replacing local protections with a weaker national floor [S2][S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that the direct effect is to reduce take-home pay for farm workers in the affected states, and that the savings accrue to their employers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to employers in the form of lower labor costs and simpler scheduling; the cost runs directly to farm workers in the form of lost overtime pay in the states with the strongest protections. There is no provision in the bill compensating workers for what they lose [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs (R-NY) introduced the bill on August 30, 2022 [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which was its only committee referral [S1][S5].
Four Republican members cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm workers in states with overtime protections are better off, because the standards the bill would have wiped out remain in force. Agricultural employers did not get the federal override they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm workers who kept their state overtime rights

for.name: Rep. Chris Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to preempt state agricultural overtime laws below a 60-hour workweek.

against.name: Rep. Robert Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no roll-call to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would have freed them from state overtime mandates below 60 hours a week, allowing longer weeks at straight-time pay. The savings come directly out of farm workers' paychecks [S2][S3].
The bill would strip states of the power to set their own maximum workweeks for agricultural workers, overriding laws they enacted on their own [S2][S3].
